title: Meeting Rooms: Sort, Then Check Neighbors
summary: Sort the meetings by start; then a clash can only be between neighbors, so one pass finds it.

takeaway.summary: Sort the meetings by start time; a clash can only happen between neighbors, so check each start against the previous meeting's end in one pass.
whenToUse: Checking whether any two intervals overlap
Any interval question where order by start makes neighbors the only candidates

scenes.narration: Your calendar has four meetings, in no particular order: 15 to 16, 9 to 10, 11 to 13, and 12 to 14. Can you attend every one of them, start to finish?
scenes.caption: Meetings 15–16, 9–10, 11–13, 12–14: can one person attend all?

scenes.narration: You could compare every meeting with every other one, which is n squared checks. Instead, sort them by start time. Then a clash can only be between neighbors, and one pass checks them all.
scenes.caption: Checking every pair of meetings is O(n²)

scenes.narration: Sorted by start time, the meetings read 9 to 10, 11 to 13, 12 to 14, and 15 to 16. Each one only needs to start after the one before it ends.
scenes.caption: Sorted by start: 9–10, 11–13, 12–14, 15–16

scenes.narration: The 11 o'clock meeting starts after the 9 o'clock one ends at 10. There's even an hour free between them, so no clash.
scenes.caption: 11–13 starts at 11, after 9–10 ends at 10: a gap

scenes.narration: But the 12 o'clock meeting starts before the 11 o'clock one ends at 13. Those two overlap for an hour, so you can't attend every meeting: the answer is false.
scenes.caption: 12–14 starts at 12, before 11–13 ends at 13: a clash

scenes.narration: That's the intervals pattern: sort by start, and the only clash worth checking is with the previous meeting. Sorting costs O(n log n); the pass after it is O(n).
scenes.caption: Sort by start, then compare each start with the previous end
